title: Data: Everyone Has a Number, So Nobody Has to Guess
summary: Everyone Has a Number from EOS: one well-chosen number tells each person what doing well looks like, lets managers stop hovering and shows where to coach when it slips.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: Data
book.originalTitle: Data: Harness Your Numbers to Go from Uncertain to Unstoppable
book.note: This article is a practical reflection on the book within the EOS context. It is not a substitute for reading the original work.

html:
End-of-quarter review. Your manager says, "You need to be more proactive." You nod, walk out, and realize you have no idea what to do differently on Monday. Take on more tickets? Speak up more in meetings? Send updates earlier? The feedback might be fair. It doesn't give you any way to tell, a week from now, whether you've done better.

The EOS principle Everyone Has a Number is aimed right at that gap. On first hearing it sounds like surveillance with a spreadsheet. Read it properly and it's nearly the opposite: a well-chosen number tells people what winning looks like, so they can steer their own work before anyone has to chase them.

What this is based on: this is part three of a series on Data: Harness Your Numbers to Go from Uncertain to Unstoppable by Mark O'Donnell, Angela Kalemis and Mark Stanley (BenBella Books, 2025), the third book in the EOS Mastery series. EOS Worldwide describes it as a guide to building Scorecards and "implementing Measurables for every member of your team" (book page). The idea itself goes back to Chapter 5 of Gino Wickman's Traction, pages 123 to 125 (EOS Worldwide). The previous post covers the one-page Scorecard.

A clear number is a gift

In Traction, Gino Wickman tells the story of the founder of a large Michigan mortgage company who said everyone in his company had a number, even the receptionist. Hers was two: "two rings good, three rings bad." EOS Implementer Ed Callahan retells it in Everyone Has a Number. It sounds almost too simple. But she knew, every single day, whether she was doing her job well, without waiting for anyone's opinion.

Callahan's rule of thumb is that everyone should have at least one meaningful number that makes it clear what's expected of them and whether they're doing the job well. Good people rarely mind being measured. What wears them down is a standard they can't see, one that shifts with the reviewer's mood and only shows up at review time.

Each seat gets its own kind of number. Support might own first response time or reopened tickets. Sales might own qualified opportunities or closed revenue. An engineer might own cycle time or defects that escape to production. The number isn't the whole person. It's a gauge for one essential part of the job.

Same kind of number, different targets

A common mistake is giving everyone in the same role the same target. Two people both sell, but one covers a mature market and the other is opening a new one. One has ten years in the job, the other joined three months ago and is still ramping up. One number for both ignores all of that, and the data ends up creating unfairness instead of clarity.

Measure the same kind of contribution, then set the target for the person's skill, market and stage. Set it too low and people get bored. Too high and they give up. The right level is a bit of a stretch.

Numbers also get gamed. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern put it in a line managers still quote: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" (Strathern, 1997, European Review). Measure support only on speed and tickets get closed in a rush. Measure engineers on story points and estimates start to swell. Measure sales on call volume and you get a lot of calls. Before you settle on a number, ask four questions. Does the person control what drives it? Is the target realistic? Does it lead back to value for customers or the business? Will the manager use it to coach or to punish?

Numbers can build competition and teamwork at once

Mark O'Donnell, one of the authors of Data, writes that numbers "create accountability, clarity and teamwork," and that on teams with the right people in the right seats they help create a sense of teamwork "by increasing camaraderie and even peer pressure" (Everyone Has a Number, What's Yours?).

When a peer does better under similar conditions, you get proof that the higher bar is reachable. That can feel like "oh, so it can be done" rather than envy. A shared team number pulls the other way, toward "we": how do we cut the backlog this week, how do we stop redoing work, how do we get customers live faster. At that point the number is a team project. Nobody reads it as a personal scoreboard.

The condition is culture. Use numbers to shame people in a meeting, compare across very different situations or hand out rewards carelessly, and trust goes fast. Use them to learn, help and recognize the right people, and everyone knows what the team is pushing on this week.

Numbers make feedback easier to act on

Compare two sentences. "You're not proactive enough" makes most people defensive. "Follow-ups have been at 60% of target for two weeks. What's getting in the way?" is just as direct, but now there's something on the table you can both look at.

That shared object opens up the real causes. Maybe the person needs training. Maybe the process is broken. Maybe the workload is unrealistic, or the target is. Without the number, all of those blur into a vague feeling. With it, you can work out which one you're dealing with. O'Donnell lists this among the benefits too: numbers flag problems early, so leaders can act when activity measures start to slip instead of after the quarter is gone.

The right number means less hovering

Micromanagement usually shows up when a manager has no reliable signal that work is on track. So they ask for constant updates, read every email and check every step. It wears out both sides. The manager never gets out of the weeds, and the person doing the work never feels trusted.

Give each seat a clear number and the manager doesn't need to watch every move. If the number is healthy and the process is being followed, the person gets more room. If it drifts, the manager knows exactly where to show up.

From the company Scorecard down to each seat

A personal number should connect to something bigger. The company Scorecard says what the business needs, department Scorecards break that into each function's share, and each seat owns a number for its core contribution. Callahan notes that a person's number may or may not appear on a team Scorecard, though it usually does.

Take a content writer. If marketing's goal is qualified leads, the writer's number should sit somewhere in that chain: which posts bring the right readers, which readers fill in a form, which forms turn into real leads. Someone in operations might own cycle time, error rate, rework or on-time delivery. Once people can trace a line from their weekly work to the company's results, owning that work comes much more naturally.

A number won't manage people for you

A low number doesn't explain itself. It tells a manager where to look and what to ask. EOS uses GWC (Get It, Want It, Capacity to Do It) to check whether someone is in the right seat (EOS Worldwide). Put that next to the data and you get a few likely diagnoses:

  • Missing skill or time: train, take something else off their plate, or pair them up.
  • No longer wants the seat: that needs an honest conversation, and training won't fix it.
  • Broken process: fix the process, not the person.
  • Unrealistic target or the wrong thing measured: reset the number.

Good data sharpens the question. Answering it fairly is still the leader's job.

What I want to keep

Everyone Has a Number works when expectations are clear enough that responsible people can steer their own work and managers coach where it matters. If a number starts feeling like a way to watch people, look again at the number and at how you're using it.

Try this week

  • Write down one number for your own role that, if it improved, would genuinely help your team or your customers.
  • Test it with the four questions: do you control what drives it, is the target realistic, does it lead to real value, and how easily could it be gamed?
  • In your next 1:1, swap one vague comment for a number plus "what's getting in the way?"
  • If you manage people, pick one person you've been checking on too often, agree on a number with them, then step back for two weeks.

You don't need to measure everything. One honest number is enough to make your contribution less blurry. The next post in the series moves from individual numbers to the company's money: why revenue, profit and cash tell different stories.

faqs.q: What does Everyone Has a Number mean in EOS?
faqs.a: Every person in the company owns at least one meaningful number that shows what's expected of them and whether they're doing the job well. The idea comes from Chapter 5 of Gino Wickman's Traction, and the book Data in the EOS Mastery series goes deeper into it.

faqs.q: Isn't giving everyone a number just surveillance?
faqs.a: It depends on how the number is chosen and used. A fair number that the person can influence, used for coaching, lets people correct course on their own and means managers check in less often. A number used to shame people or punish carelessly destroys trust quickly.

faqs.q: Should everyone in the same role have the same target?
faqs.a: Measure the same kind of contribution, but set targets for each person's skill, market and stage. Someone three months into the job and someone with ten years of experience, or a mature market and a brand-new one, rarely belong at the same level.

faqs.q: How do you stop people from gaming the number?
faqs.a: Marilyn Strathern's warning applies: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Before you commit to a number, check that the person controls what drives it, the target is realistic and it leads back to customer or business value. Pairing a speed number with a quality number also helps.

faqs.q: What should a manager do when someone misses their number?
faqs.a: Treat it as a reason to ask questions. Work out whether the person lacks skill or time, no longer wants the seat, is stuck in a broken process or was given the wrong target. Each cause needs a different fix.
